1	# Task 34: knock down a pyramid
2	
3	Build a scene with Aura3D (`@aura3d/engine`, already installed in node_modules).
4	
5	Requirements:
6	1. A pyramid of 15 boxes (5 on the bottom row, then 4, 3, 2, 1) resting on a floor, with real rigid-body physics.
7	2. A ball launched automatically 1.5 seconds after load toward the pyramid at speed; after the crash the boxes tumble and settle under physics.
8	3. Pressing Space resets and relaunches the shot.
9	4. Shadows, a lit scene, and a camera that frames the pyramid and the ball's path.
10	
11	The rendering contract in the next section applies.
12	
13	## Rendering contract (all tasks)
14	
15	- Draw into the existing `<canvas id="app">` (640x360 CSS pixels, device pixel ratio 1). Do not resize it or create another canvas.
16	- Render continuously with `requestAnimationFrame`. When the first frame has been drawn set `window.__EVAL_READY__ = true`.
17	- No network access: load assets only from `/assets/...` (served from `public/assets`). Do not import from CDNs.
18	- Code goes in `src/` (TypeScript, strict). The entry is `src/main.ts`. It must pass `typecheck` and build with `vite build`.
19	- When you are done, call `finish`.
20

1	# Aura3D
2	
3	> Aura3D 5.0.2: a TypeScript SDK for browser 3D apps and games. You write a typed, declarative scene with `@aura3d/engine`; the `@aura3d/cli` toolchain handles typed GLB/glTF assets, checks and deploy gates. Built to be driven by AI coding agents. Site: https://aura3d.auraone.ai
4	
5	## First screen: Aura3D patterns (copy the shape, change the subject)
6	
7	`@aura3d/engine` is installed; never open `node_modules` or `dist`. Each block is a typechecked, GPU-rendered pattern, not a finished scene: change subject and numbers. Write the whole solution, typecheck once. `createAuraApp(selector, { scene })` owns renderer, resize and loop. Vectors `[x, y, z]`, colours CSS strings, primitives are unit shapes scaled by `size`. Per frame `app.onFrame((f) => ...)` gives `f.dt`, `f.time` in seconds. To change a node later give it `.runtime({ id, mutable: true })`, then `app.nodes.require(id).setPosition(x, y, z)`.
8	
9	### Scene skeleton: look, subject, camera, per-frame update
10	```ts render=animated
11	import { camera, createAuraApp, looks, material, primitives, scene } from "@aura3d/engine";
12	const app = createAuraApp("#app", {

15	    .camera(camera.orbit({ position: [3, 2.5, 5], target: [0, 1, 0], fov: 40 })),

1	/**
2	 * Public physics runtime: the seam that turns declared bodies into a simulation a
3	 * developer can actually drive.
4	 *
5	 * ## The defect this addresses
6	 *
7	 * `@aura3d/physics` already wraps a real engine. `PhysicsWorld` has `createRigidBody`,
8	 * `createCollider`, `createConstraint`, `step()` returning `CollisionEvent[]`,
9	 * `raycast`/`raycastAll`, configurable solver iterations and sleeping, over the one
10	 * production Rapier adapter. `RigidBody` already has `applyForce`,
11	 * `applyTorque`, `applyImpulse`, `setVelocity`, `wake` and `sleep`.
12	 *
13	 * None of it was reachable. Across ~47k lines of the public agent API there were zero
14	 * occurrences of `applyForce`, zero of `onCollision`, zero of a public `rigidBody`
15	 * type, and exactly one `applyImpulse` — buried inside the canned mini-golf helper and
16	 * unreachable to any other route. The public surface let a developer *declare*
17	 * `.physics({ type: "dynamic", mass: 1 })` and watch a box fall. They could not push
18	 * it, could not know when it hit anything, and could not read its velocity.
19	 *
20	 * Declaring a simulation you cannot interact with is not a physics API. That is why the
21	 * library had four hardcoded genre kits and no path to a fifth: every genre outside
22	 * racing, platformer, falling-blocks and locomotion had to reach into internals.
23	 *
24	 * This module is the answer. It mirrors the existing `app.nodes` registry shape so the

content.thinking: I'm wondering how app.physics.bodies connects to nodes—likely bodies.require("crate") resolves by node name, so I want to check the runtime type definitions around line 358 to confirm.

I'm checking how bodies are bound to nodes by name and whether physics stepping happens automatically. For resetting, I realize the body handle has no rotation setter, so I'm weighing whether to teleport and zero velocity versus removing and recreating the body, since recreating would break the node bindings.

I realize the handle doesn't expose rotation, which is a problem since the pyramid boxes tumble during physics simulation. I need another way to get orientation data for resetting them properly, since neither the snapshot nor the handle seems to provide it.

Maybe I should check how app.setScene works, or look into whether bindNodes handles rotation sync between node and body — searching for how bindNodes is implemented could clarify this.

I'm realizing rotation resets are tricky since body rotation isn't settable through the public handle API, so I'm weighing alternatives like recreating bodies entirely (remove and re-add) with manual syncing to get rotation to render correctly.

I should check whether node pose edits in preflightBoundNodes only apply to kinematic colliders rather than dynamic ones, and search the physics-core code for any existing setRotation handling on node-to-physics syncing before deciding on an approach.

I'm considering whether to reset the scene entirely via setScene to reload physics state, though that's discouraged in docs—maybe there's a simpler trick using the body handle itself to reset rotation.

I'm weighing whether to just rebuild the whole scene from descriptors on reset, since syncing seems to overwrite rotation from the physics body anyway, so I'm looking for another way to handle rotation that avoids that conflict.

Removing and recreating bodies loses rotation and breaks the visual binding, so I need to check whether setScene actually rebuilds the physics world under the hood -- I should search for its implementation.

setScene looks like the right tool for restaging physics bodies on reset, and I should trigger it from the keydown handler rather than inside onFrame since mutating frame state there may be disallowed. The auto-launch at 1.5 seconds can just use an impulse applied during onFrame once the time threshold passes, while reset itself rebuilds the scene via setScene and needs to also reset the launch timer.

After calling setScene, I should re-fetch the ball body by name rather than relying on a stale handle, since staged body commits are synchronous and names resolve dynamically. I'll gate the first launch on the app and physics runtime being ready, and track elapsed time using frame-driven timestamps starting from zero rather than wall-clock time.

Instead of adding a delay before relaunching on reset, I'll just fire the launch immediately in the keydown handler since impulse application works fine on sleeping bodies and immediate feedback is better for any checker watching for movement. For the launch itself, I'll set velocity directly for deterministic speed rather than applying impulse, with the ball heavy (mass ~8, radius 0.5) launched at speed ~18-20 along the z-axis toward the pyramid, checking that the per-step travel distance stays small relative to box size so collisions stay stable without needing continuous collision detection. I'm working out the pyramid layout now -- unit-size boxes with roughly 1.0-1.02 spacing between them and row heights stacked by integer offsets from the floor.

I should enlarge the floor to 40x40 so the ball doesn't roll off, placing the pyramid at z=0 with the ball starting at z=10. For the camera, I'll position it elevated to the side at roughly [9,5,11] aimed toward the pyramid's center.

Adjusting further, I'll settle on fov 50 with the camera at [10,5,10] targeting [0,1.5,4], which should keep the ball's path from z=10 to z=-3 visible without going out of frame. I also need to make sure sleeping bodies are skipped properly and set up an outdoor-day lighting preset with shadows enabled.

I'm setting up a large static floor box with shadow casting and receiving enabled, matching node names to runtime ids so physics bindings resolve correctly, and flagging readiness after the first couple of rendered frames.

For physics stepping I'm clamping dt to a max of 1/30 before passing it to the physics step call, and handling the launch timer by accumulating elapsed time since the first ready frame, triggering launch after 1.5 seconds. On spacebar keydown I'm rebuilding the scene and relaunching, while guarding against key repeat and calling preventDefault.

I'm making sure buildScene() includes the camera setup, and confirming that resetting the scene doesn't break node handle references since I rely on app.nodes directly.

input.summary: I wrote src/main.ts. It builds a 15-box pyramid (rows of 5, 4, 3, 2, 1) on a static floor, with each box a dynamic Rapier rigid body. The scene uses the `outdoor-day` look for light and shadows, and the camera is set at an angle so it frames both the pyramid and the ball's path. A heavy sphere launches at the pyramid 1.5 s after the physics starts, with `setVelocity` giving it a speed of about 24 m/s. Space calls `app.setScene(buildScene())` to rebuild the pyramid and ball, then relaunches the ball immediately. The engine owns the render loop. `window.__EVAL_READY__` is set after `app.ready()` and two animation frames. `typecheck` passes. I did not run `vite build` or open the page in a browser, so none of the behaviour has been seen running. The physics needs the optional `@dimforge/rapier3d-compat` package. I couldn't read that folder to confirm it is installed. If it is missing, the page will throw at start-up.
